transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, I'm here because I spend most of my day going back over the same things in the house. The outlets, the locks, my tools... even the dust. I just keep checking and fixing them, again and again. I do it until I'm completely worn out, and even then, I still don't feel sure enough to just leave it alone. It's basically taking up my whole day.
Before you feel the urge to check these things, do you have unwanted thoughts or worries that pop into your head that make you feel like you need to check them?

Yeah, that's exactly it. Even when I know for a fact I did a job right, these... these ugly thoughts just keep jumping into my head. I'll start worrying that a loose wire I missed is going to burn the whole house down, or that a nail I left somewhere is going to hurt my wife. I try to just push them out of my mind, but... they just come right back, and they feel even stronger than before.

When you have these thoughts about the wire causing a fire or the nail hurting your wife, do you believe that these things are actually likely to happen, or do you recognize that these worries are probably not realistic even though they feel very strong?

I'm not really sure how to answer that. I mean... I guess I haven't really stopped to think about whether it's actually realistic or not. When the thought pops up, it just feels so strong that I feel like I can't take the chance. I don't really know if I actually believe the house is going to burn down right that second, I just know the worry is there and I have to go check it.

When you're not actively checking these things, and you step back and think about it logically, do you recognize that your worry about the house burning down or the nail hurting your wife is excessive or unreasonable, even though it doesn't feel that way when the thought hits you?

I'm honestly not sure. I don't think I ever really get a chance to step back from it like that. Even when I'm sitting down and not physically checking anything, my mind is still going over it all. So... I don't really know if I see it as unreasonable or excessive. I just know the feeling doesn't ever really turn off enough for me to look at it logically.

If I told you that most people wouldn't need to check their outlets, locks, and tools repeatedly throughout the day, and that the actual risk of these things causing harm is very small, would you be able to agree with that, or does it still feel like you genuinely need to keep checking no matter what?

I mean... I hear what you're saying. If you tell me the risk is small, I guess I can agree with that logically. But... I don't know, it still feels like I genuinely need to keep checking. No matter what someone tells me, or what I try to tell myself, that feeling that I have to go look just doesn't go away. So, yeah, I can agree with the facts, but it doesn't change how I feel about needing to check.

When you're calm and relaxed, away from the checking, and you think about these fears - like the house burning down from a wire - do you recognize that thought as unreasonable or silly, even if you still feel the urge to check anyway?

I don't think I ever really get calm and relaxed enough to look at it like that. The fear is just always there, in the back of my mind. Even if I try to tell myself it's silly, it doesn't feel silly. It feels real. So I guess I don't really see it as unreasonable, because the feeling is just too strong.

If you really think about it carefully, do you believe there's actually a realistic chance that a loose wire you might have missed could burn down your house, or do you know deep down that this is very unlikely to actually happen?

I honestly don't know. I mean, when I try to really think about it carefully... I just don't have that feeling deep down that it's unlikely. My brain just tells me there is a realistic chance. It feels completely possible to me, so... no, I can't really say I know it won't happen. It just feels too real to ignore.

If you were to see a professional electrician inspect your house and tell you that everything is safe and properly installed, would you be able to believe them and feel reassured, or would you still feel the need to check again?

I don't think that would help, honestly. I'd probably just think... well, what if the electrician missed something? Or what if something shifted or broke right after they left? Even if they told me it was completely safe, I'd still have that voice in my head telling me I need to go look for myself just to be sure. So, no, I don't think I'd be reassured. I'd still have to check.

When you're having these checking urges, do you ever have a moment where you can step back and recognize that your fear doesn't match reality, or does it always feel completely convincing and real to you?

I don't think I ever really have a moment like that. It... it always just feels completely real to me. When I get the urge to check, I can't just step back from it. The fear is just right there, and it's convincing every single time. I don't really look at it and think it doesn't match reality, because to me, right then, it just feels like a fact.
If I asked your closest family member or friend whether they think your worry about the house burning down from a wire is reasonable, what do you think they would say, and would you agree with them?

My mom, probably... she'd say it's completely unreasonable. She's told me before that I'm overreacting and that the house is fine. But... no, I wouldn't agree with her. I know she thinks it's silly, but she doesn't see what I see, or feel that... that danger. To me, it's still a real threat, no matter what she says.

When you really think about it logically and carefully, separate from how the fear feels in the moment, do you actually believe there is a real danger, or do you know it's probably not true but the feeling just overrides that knowledge?

I... I don't really know how to separate it, to be honest. Even when I try to think about it logically, it still feels like a real danger. I don't have this... this knowledge that it's probably not true. The fear and the reality just feel like the exact same thing to me. So, yeah, I do believe there's a real danger.

Let me ask this a different way: If you had to bet money on whether a loose wire you might have missed will actually cause a fire in your house, how confident would you be that it will happen? Would you say you're very confident it will, somewhat confident, or not confident at all?

I'd say... I would be very confident it will happen. I mean, if I actually had to bet money on it, yeah, I'm very confident. Like I was just saying, it doesn't feel like a 'maybe' to me. If I miss a bad wire, I really truly believe it's going to start a fire.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient meets criteria for OCD with poor insight (F42.2). Presents with clear obsessions (intrusive thoughts about fires, injury from missed items) and compulsions (repetitive checking of outlets, locks, tools). Critically, the patient demonstrates poor insight—he endorses genuine belief in the danger ('very confident' a missed wire will cause fire, 'feels like a fact') rather than recognizing obsessions as excessive/unreasonable. He cannot reliably step back and identify thoughts as irrational even when prompted, and maintains conviction despite external reassurance and logical contradiction. This poor/absent insight pattern is characteristic of F42.2 (OCD with poor insight) rather than F42.1 (good insight). Functional impairment is severe, consuming most of his day.
